quiz.q: In the watchman analogy, what does the API gateway do?
options: Sits between consumers and the API, checks each request against the policies and rejects invalid ones
Stores API specifications so consumers can discover them
Runs the Mule flows on a CloudHub worker
Generates RAML from the API implementation
quiz.explain: Like a watchman at a house, the gateway checks whether the request comes from the right client and follows the policies; if not, it is rejected at the gateway before reaching the API.

quiz.q: Your organisation has Mule APIs and also Java/Spring Boot APIs, and wants one gateway for all of them. Which gateway fits?
options: Mule Gateway
Flex Gateway
A proxy application
API Autodiscovery
quiz.explain: Flex Gateway is an independent gateway that protects Mule and non-Mule APIs. Mule Gateway is embedded in the Mule runtime and protects Mule apps only.

quiz.q: Which statement about Mule Gateway is correct?
options: It must be installed on its own separate server by admins
It is embedded in the Mule runtime, so nothing extra has to be set up
It protects Mule and non-Mule APIs
It is the same product as Kong
quiz.explain: Mule Gateway runs inside the app's worker as part of the Mule runtime. Installing on a separate server describes Flex Gateway.

quiz.q: What is the main cost of choosing "Deploy a proxy application" instead of "Connect to existing application (basic endpoint)"?
options: The API can no longer have policies
The proxy is a separate app with its own workers, CPU and memory
The app must be redeployed for every request
Auto-Discovery stops working
quiz.explain: A proxy is another application in Runtime Manager, so it consumes its own resources. It makes sense for exposed experience APIs, but wastes resources for internal process/system APIs.

quiz.q: A deployed app must get its policies from API Manager. Which two pieces make this work?
options: The platform client ID/secret (to authenticate) and the API instance ID via Auto-Discovery (to find the API)
The consumer's client ID/secret and the HTTP Listener port
The mule.env property and the secure.key property
The RAML file and the asset version
quiz.explain: Client ID/secret = communication with the control plane; instance ID + auto-discovery = finding the API so its policies are downloaded.

quiz.q: The platform client ID/secret given at deployment come from where?
options: The Client ID Enforcement contract of each consumer
The environment's credentials in Access Management → Environments
The API Autodiscovery global element
Exchange asset details
quiz.explain: They are the environment's credentials, which are different from the per-consumer credentials used by the Client ID Enforcement policy.

quiz.q: You just saved a new API instance in API Manager but have not deployed the app with Auto-Discovery yet. What status does it show?
options: Active
Unregistered
Deprecated
Pending approval
quiz.explain: A new instance is Unregistered; it becomes Active once the deployed app connects to it through Auto-Discovery.

quiz.q: When configuring the API Autodiscovery global element, what goes in the Flow name field?
options: The main flow (with the Listener and router)
The error handler flow
The first sub-flow in the project
The name of the API in Exchange
quiz.explain: The API ID gets the property placeholder for the instance ID, and Flow name points to the main flow that has the Listener and APIkit router.

quiz.q: What is the main weakness of the Basic Authentication policy?
options: It generates a new token on every call, which is slow
The same username/password is shared by all consumers, so you can't tell them apart
It only works on Flex Gateway
It requires a proxy application
quiz.explain: Basic auth uses one generic credential for everyone; it can be shared further and gives no traceability, so it is less secure.

quiz.q: Which policy gives each consumer its own credential pair so you can track which client called?
options: Basic Authentication – Simple
Client ID Enforcement
Header injection
Message logging
quiz.explain: Client ID Enforcement generates a separate client ID and client secret for each consumer (by default from the Anypoint client provider).

quiz.q: Why should an externally exposed API not rely only on Client ID Enforcement?
options: Client ID/secret are static, while OAuth issues a new token each time
Client ID Enforcement cannot be applied to experience APIs
It only works with a proxy
It rejects all requests with 429
quiz.explain: The client ID/secret are the same on every call; OAuth generates a new token each time and is more secure, so the experience layer gets HTTPS + OAuth.

quiz.q: In the Day 31 policy catalogue, which category do Client ID enforcement and CORS belong to?
options: Security
Quality of service
Compliance
Transformation
quiz.explain: Client ID enforcement and CORS were listed under Compliance. Rate limiting and spike control are Quality of service; Basic auth and OAuth are Security.

cards.back: A layer between consumers and APIs that enforces policies (authentication, rate limits, …) and forwards only valid requests — the "watchman".
**Flex**: independent, installed separately, protects Mule and non-Mule APIs. **Mule Gateway**: embedded in the Mule runtime, protects Mule apps only.
When you only have Mule APIs — no extra servers or configuration needed.
A separate app deployed in Runtime Manager in front of the real API. Costs its own workers/CPU/memory, so use it only for externally exposed experience APIs.
API Manager connects to the already deployed app via auto-discovery — no extra application.
Unique ID API Manager gives an API instance (100 APIs → 100 IDs). The app uses it via Auto-Discovery to find its API and download policies.
A global element that links a deployed Mule app to its API instance in API Manager using the instance ID, so policies are fetched and enforced.
API ID: the instance ID property placeholder (e.g. `${autodiscovery.id}`); Flow name: the main flow with the Listener and router.

cards.front: How does a deployed app talk to API Manager?
cards.back: It authenticates with the environment's **platform client ID/secret** and identifies its API via the **auto-discovery instance ID**.
The environment's credentials (Access Management → Environments) that let the runtime authenticate to the control plane — not the per-consumer credentials of Client ID Enforcement.
API instance status before / after the deployed app connects to it through Auto-Discovery.
① Publish spec to Exchange → ② create API instance in API Manager (instance ID) → ③ configure Autodiscovery in the app → ④ deploy to Runtime Manager.
System that issues consumer client IDs/secrets for Client ID Enforcement — default is **Anypoint**.
Consumer sends a username and password; the gateway checks them. One credential shared by everyone — weak and not traceable.
Each consumer gets its own client ID and secret; the gateway validates the pair. More secure and traceable, but more steps.

cards.front: Basic auth vs. client ID enforcement
cards.back: Basic auth: one shared username/password, less security, fewer steps. Client ID: separate pair per consumer, more security (know who called), more effort.

cards.front: Which policies on experience vs. process/system APIs?
cards.back: Experience (external): **HTTPS + OAuth**. Process/system (internal): lighter policies like basic auth or client ID enforcement — regulated industries (e.g. banks audited by RBI) may need at least basic auth.

cards.front: Why not only client ID enforcement on external APIs?
cards.back: Client ID/secret are static (same every call); OAuth generates a new token each time, so it is more secure.

Security (OAuth, JWT, threat protection, basic auth, IP lists), Quality of service (caching, spike control, rate limiting), Compliance (client ID, CORS), Troubleshooting (message logging), Transformation (header injection/removal).
Rate limiting: fixed window, extra requests rejected with **429 Too Many Requests**. Spike control: sliding window, extra requests queued/delayed and retried.
Client ID + rate limit per tier, e.g. Silver 1 req/min, Gold 2 req/min, Diamond 5 req/min.

cards.front: How often are custom policies needed?
cards.back: Rarely — 90–95% of the time MuleSoft's existing policies are used; custom policies are advanced and rare.
